title: Why the Ocean Is Salty
meta_description: Discover how rock weathering, rivers, seafloor reactions and long-term chemical balances make seawater salty, with salinity varying around the planet.
author: Suraj Dahal
key_takeaways: Rainwater and weathering release dissolved ions from rocks; rivers carry many of those ions to the sea, while hydrothermal circulation and seafloor processes also alter ocean chemistry.
Sodium and chloride are the dominant dissolved ions in seawater, though seawater contains a mixture of salts rather than only table salt.
Average ocean salinity is often approximated as 35 parts per thousand, but evaporation, precipitation, river input, ice formation and melting create regional differences.
Ocean salinity reflects a balance between inputs and removal processes over long periods; it is not simply the result of water evaporating once and leaving every dissolved substance behind.
